p: Quick start on the hosted service
t: Sign up, add a board with one command and boot it from the network. No server to install. We run the server at app.orchestrator.sh. An account is free for 10 devices. To run the server on your own machine instead, see Quick start on your own server.

p: Quick start on the hosted service
t: - A Raspberry Pi 4, Pi 5, Compute Module 4 or Compute Module 5 on wired Ethernet. - Outbound access from the board to app.orchestrator.sh on ports 443 and 50051, and to boot.orchestrator.sh on port 80 for network boot. Nothing has to be opened towards the board.

p: Quick start on the hosted service
t: Open app.orchestrator.sh and click Sign up with Google . To use a password instead, sign up with your e-mail and click the link in the confirmation message. Until you do, the app shows a reminder instead of your account. Once you're in, you can add a passkey under your account settings and sign in with it from then on.

p: Quick start on the hosted service
h: Add a board that already runs Linux
t: 1. Click Add node and open the One command tab. 2. Click Generate command , then Copy command . 3. Run the line on the board as a user with sudo. It needs 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS, Debian or Ubuntu. 4. The board shows up in Nodes as PENDING . Check the HW serial and click Approve . A board with nothing on it joins another way: flash its bootloader from the browser over USB, or boot it from a provisioning card (Adding a device).

p: Quick start on the hosted service
h: Make it boot from the network
t: A board added with one command keeps its old bootloader. Point it at the server once: 1. Open the node, go to Advanced → Bootloader / EEPROM and click Update bootloader . 2. Click Reboot to apply . From now on the board asks the server first on every boot. The server sends the recovery system when you ask for it. Otherwise, or if the server can't be reached, the board boots its own drive.

p: Quick start on the hosted service
t: 1. Go to Operations → Install images and upload an image. A hosted account holds up to 3 images of up to 15 GB each. 2. Open the node, click Reboot to recovery and wait for RECOVERY . 3. Follow Installing an operating system from step 3.

p: Quick start on the hosted service
t: Write to sales@orchestrator.sh. Devices you already added keep working when a limit is reached. Only new ones wait. Next: Adding a device.

p: Quick start on your own server
t: Install the server with one command and sign in. Uptime Orchestrator manages a fleet of Raspberry Pi boards from one web UI. You adopt devices, install operating systems on them over the network, and control who logs in and what runs on them.

p: Quick start on your own server
t: - An x86-64 or arm64 machine or VM running Debian or Ubuntu, with 4 GB of RAM and disk space for your OS images. A Raspberry Pi 5 with an SSD works as the server. The installer installs Docker on Ubuntu. On another distribution, install Docker first. - Root, or a user who can use sudo . - A name or address for the server. On a local network, ports 80 and 50051 must be free. From the internet, you need a public DNS name that points at the machine, with ports 80 , 443 and 50051 open. - Free loopback ports 8080 , 8088 and 50052 . - Devices: Raspberry Pi 4, Raspberry Pi 5, Compute Module 4 or Compute Module 5, on Ethernet. Warning: The name or address is written into every device you adopt and into the bootloader of every network-booted device. Pick one that won't change, and on a local network reserve the machine's address in your router's DHCP settings first. A self-hosted install manages 25 devices free (the device limit).

p: Quick start on your own server
t: On the server, run: curl -fsSL https://get.orchestrator.sh sh It asks a few questions, runs its checks, and asks Install now? (y/n) before it changes anything. - How will your devices and your browser reach this server? Pick 1 for a local network or 2 for the internet. - Name or address the devices should use (local network). Accept the offered name or give the machine's address. A .local name is refused because a Pi bootloader can't resolve it. - DNS name that points at this machine and an email for Let's Encrypt (internet). The email can stay empty. - Set up network boot? (y/n) Answer y if you want to boot blank devices from the server and install their OS from the web UI. It downloads a recovery image of about 100 MB and creates a signing key. - Email address the owner signs in with. This becomes the first account, and it owns the server. Everything goes into ./orchestrator under the directory you ran the command from. Every question is also a flag for an unattended run ( install.sh --help , INSTALL.md). If a step fails, run the installer again with the same answers. It keeps what it already wrote and skips finished steps. If the certificate doesn't arrive, check that the DNS name resolves to the machine's public address from outside and that port 80 is open, then run docker restart orchestrator-proxy . The run ends with the address to open and where the owner password is. It also names two files to copy somewhere safe, off the machine. Warning: Without secrets/secrets_encryption_key a database backup can't be read. Without data/eeprom-keys/privkey.pem (created with network boot) you can never sign for your network-booted devices again.

p: Quick start on your own server
t: 1. Open the address the installer printed. 2. Enter the owner email in Your Email and the contents of ./orchestrator/owner-password in Password , then click Sign In . You land on Nodes . It is empty on a new server; the picture shows one with devices already added. Sign-up is closed, so colleagues join by invitation (Team and security).

p: Quick start on your own server
t: 1. Click the round badge with your initials at the top right, then Account . 2. Expand Password . 3. Type the new password in New password and Confirm password . It needs at least 8 characters. 4. Click Save password , paste the generated password into Current password , and click Confirm . 5. Delete the file on the server with rm ./orchestrator/owner-password . The installer names the account "My Account". To rename it, open the same menu, then Team Management → Organization → Rename . Two-step verification and Passkeys are on the same tab. If you lose the password and the server has no mail relay, reset it from the server with --reset-password (INSTALL.md).

p: Quick start on your own server
t: Go to Nodes → Add node , as the installer's final message says. Add a device covers each way in.
Where each section is and how to read the Nodes list. Find your way around the web UI. The list below links each top-level section to its page in this guide.

- Nodes lists your devices. Click a row to open its panel (The node panel), or click Add node to adopt one (Add a device). - Organization holds your units and the policies they set (Organization and units). - Credentials controls who can log in to devices (Access and credentials). - Secrets holds values for devices and playbooks, and adoption tokens (Secrets and variables). - Operations has playbooks and their runs (Playbooks) and your OS images (Install an operating system). - Utilities keeps software such as security updates configured on nodes (Utilities). - Status lists nodes that need you and the command history (Status and audit). - The round badge at the top right opens your password, sign-in settings and team (Team and security). The Organizational Units sidebar on the left filters most pages to one unit. You create and rename units on the Organization page.

The coloured bar at the left of each row and the word under the name give the node's status. Colour Status Green ONLINE Violet RECOVERY , the network-boot recovery system Yellow with PENDING AWAITING APPROVAL Yellow Restarting, installing an OS, shutting down, ready for adoption Orange MAINTENANCE , a command is running Blue FLASHING the bootloader, or BUSY Red OFFLINE , or the last adoption or OS install failed Grey UNREACHABLE , or ADOPTING Hover over a badge next to a name, such as REBOOT PENDING or UNDER-VOLTAGE , to see what it means.

Type in the search box to match a name, IP address, serial, OS or notes. The dropdowns narrow by status, board, RAM and disk, and they combine with the unit selected in the sidebar. Every live node falls under one of Online , Recovery , Maintenance or Offline , so if a node seems missing, step through them.

1. Click Select / Assign to unit next to the page title. 2. Tick the nodes, or click Select all . 3. Open Assign to unit and pick a unit, or Remove from unit (Unassigned) . 4. Click Done . In selection mode you can also drag the ticked nodes onto a unit in the sidebar. Actions in the same toolbar reboots, runs a playbook on, or deletes the selected nodes.

What boots a board, what runs on it, and which step checks which. A board boots a small recovery system from your server. An agent inside it writes the operating system and then keeps the board managed. This page follows that path and says what is checked at each step.

Part Where it runs What it does Server Your machine, or our hosted service Web UI and API, the device channel, OS image storage, and the signer that prepares bootloaders Bootloader The board's EEPROM Holds the server's name and public key, and fetches the recovery system Recovery image The board's RAM A 98 MB Linux system with the agent inside. It does not touch the drive by itself Agent Recovery, and later the installed OS Connects out to the server, runs your commands and reports back The board connects out to the server, so it can sit behind NAT.

The board uses the HTTP boot built into the Raspberry Pi bootloader: 1. It gets an ordinary address from the network's DHCP server. 2. Its bootloader asks the server, by name, for the recovery image and its signature over HTTP on port 80. 3. It checks the signature against the key it holds, loads the image into RAM and starts it. Nothing changes on the router, and the server can be on another network or on the internet. Plain HTTP is enough because the bootloader checks the signature: an image signed by another key does not boot. The bootloader learns the server's name and key once per board: from the browser over USB, with a provisioning card, or from a board that already runs Linux (Adding a device).

1. You approve the board by its hardware serial. 2. The server prepares a bootloader for that board and the agent writes it. 3. The board boots the recovery system from the server. 4. The agent streams the OS image you picked onto the drive. 5. The agent installs itself into the new system with the board's own credential. 6. The board boots from its drive and reports in. Over the internet this takes about six minutes on a Compute Module 4 or 5 (Installing an operating system).

A board whose drive cannot be booted goes round its boot order and asks the server again, about every 30 seconds. Set its Boot behavior to Recovery and the next request gets the recovery system. No power cycle is needed. In two runs a board with a wiped drive was back in recovery 57 and 73 seconds after the switch. A board whose system starts and then hangs does not ask again by itself. It needs a reboot: a power cycle, or a watchdog you armed beforehand (Hardware and the watchdog).

Step Checked by How Recovery image Bootloader RSA signature made with the server's own key, created when you turn network boot on Agent in recovery Bootloader The agent is part of the signed image. Recovery downloads no code OS image Agent SHA-256 sent with the install command. The agent writes the first part of the image last, so a drive that fails the check never becomes bootable Agent package Server, then agent Signature made on hardware keys kept offline. The server checks a release on import, the agent checks the package before installing it Commands and secrets TLS The device channel uses TLS whenever the server has an https address The agent carries the public keys that verify agent packages, so a board installs only agents signed for the build it runs. A fork built from source replaces that key set and signs its own releases (ARTIFACT-SIGNING.md).

- This is not Secure Boot. The bootloader's key is stored in the EEPROM, not fused into the board. Someone who holds the board, or has root on it, can write another key. - The installed OS boots unsigned. The signature covers the recovery system. The board boots the image you installed as it is. - OS images are not signed. The checksum is only as trustworthy as the channel that carried it. On a local server over plain HTTP, that channel is not encrypted. - The server is trusted. Whoever controls your server controls your boards. Note: A local server without a certificate sends commands and secrets unencrypted. Use it on a network you trust, or give the server a DNS name and let the installer get a certificate. Next: Adding a device.

Turn a Raspberry Pi into a managed node, then approve it. Adopt a device so it shows up in Nodes and you can manage it. Open Nodes , click Add node , and pick the tab that fits your device. Your device Tab Already runs a 64-bit Debian or Ubuntu One command A board you can connect over USB in boot mode USB flash Blank, and you can put a card into it Master image (provisioning card) The device needs Ethernet and outbound access to the server on port 50051, plus port 80 for a server on your local network or 443 for one on the internet. The USB and card ways bring their own recovery system, so you install an OS afterwards (Installing an operating system).

h: Run one command on a device that already runs Linux
t: 1. Open the One command tab. 2. Type a Token name if you want one, such as workshop batch . 3. Click Generate command , then Copy command . 4. Run the line on the device as a user with sudo. The script installs the agent and tells you when it has connected. On a fresh system it first waits for the system's own package upgrade to finish and tells you so. The device needs arm64 with systemd , dpkg , curl or wget , and openssl . The token works for 7 days and for several devices. You find it under Secrets → Tokens (Secrets and variables). To remove the agent later, run curl -fsSL <server address /uninstall.sh sudo sh with the same http:// or https:// address as in the install command.

h: Flash a board from the browser
t: This writes the board's bootloader so it boots from your server. Use Chrome or Edge over HTTPS. On Windows, install the WinUSB driver first as the tab explains. 1. Put the board into USB boot mode and connect it to your computer. 2. Click Connect device and pick the board. Board serial fills in. 3. Type a Node name if you want one. 4. Click Flash EEPROM and don't unplug the board until the green notice appears. 5. Unplug USB, connect Ethernet and power the board on. The node arrives already approved. Power the board on within the days the tab names (30 by default). Your account holds the serial only for that time. After it, another account can claim the serial. If none has, the node still binds the board when it connects.

h: Boot a blank device from a provisioning card
t: 1. Open the Master image tab. 2. Pick an SSH key for the new nodes, and set Expires At to change the default of 7 days. 3. Click Download SD Image . Each click creates a new token. 4. Format the card as FAT32 on an MBR partition table. In macOS Disk Utility, choose View → Show All Devices , select the card itself, and erase it as MS-DOS (FAT) with scheme Master Boot Record . 5. Unzip the bundle into the root of the card. 6. Insert the card and power the device on. 7. Leave the card in until you have approved the node and it shows RECOVERY . Then move the card to the next device. To prepare a card for one named device, use the Single node tab instead. Create the node, then click Download SD image in its panel. That node arrives already approved. Warning: Treat a provisioning card as a secret. It can enrol devices into your account, and every device it sets up leaves a credential on it. Warning: A device that another server managed boots its own drive before the card, so it never reads your card. Remove the drive while the card does its work, or flash the board from the browser.

A device from One command or Master image shows a yellow bar and PENDING in Nodes . Click it, check the HW serial , and click Approve . Approval applies the node's access and utilities at once. By default, a device running the recovery system from a provisioning card also gets a bootloader that boots from your server. A device added with One command keeps its bootloader. If that device already network-boots from this server, open Properties and set Boot behavior to Local OS before its next reboot: left on Inherit , it boots the recovery system. Next: install an operating system on the node.

Write an OS image to a node's drive from the recovery system and boot it. Install or reinstall an OS on an approved node. The node boots a small recovery system from your server, the agent in it writes the image to the node's drive, and the node then boots the new system from its own disk.

h: Install an OS on a node
t: 1. Go to Operations → Install images , click Upload image , fill in Title and Version , choose the file, and click Done . Use .img , .iso , .xz or .zst . 2. Open the node, go to Actions , click Reboot to recovery and confirm. Wait until the node turns violet and shows RECOVERY . 3. Click Install OS in the Provisioning group. 4. Check the Image and pick the Target Device . The node's default image is preselected and marked default . An image without an uploaded file is listed but can't be chosen. Read the device path, because a board with a card or eMMC lists those too. 5. Click Install OS and confirm. This erases the target drive. Progress shows in Command history . 6. Click Install Agent , choose the same Target Device , keep the other defaults and start it. It takes seconds. 7. Open Properties and set Boot behavior to Local OS . 8. Click Actions → Reboot . The node comes back ONLINE in the new system with the image's default hostname, which you can change with Actions → Change hostname . A fresh system usually gets a new address from your router, so check the node's IP before you connect over SSH. If an install fails, the node's boot target switches to Recovery so it doesn't boot a half-written disk. Run Install OS and Install Agent again. Reboot to recovery works once. The next reboot goes back to the node's saved boot target. It is refused when the node is offline or when its boot order doesn't reach network boot. For a faster install of a vendor .xz file, use Repack to multi-block XZ in the image's settings. Size limits are set by whoever runs the server (OS-IMAGES.md).

Local OS boots the system on the node's drive. Recovery boots the recovery system from your server. Set it in one of three places: - on the node, in Properties → Boot behavior - on a unit, in its Policies tab on the Organization page - for the whole account, in Organization → Account defaults → Boot → Target A node on Inherit takes its unit's value, then the parent unit's, then the account default. The account default is Recovery until you change it (Organizational units and policies). Warning: A node set to Local OS with nothing on its drive boots into nothing. Set Boot behavior to Recovery and power-cycle it.

Network boot works because each node's bootloader knows your server's address and key. It is written when you flash the board from the browser, or by default when you approve a device booted from a provisioning card. Open Advanced → Bootloader / EEPROM and click Update bootloader when it shows Update available or a banner says the bootloader isn't set up for this server. Then click Reboot to apply . Warning: Don't power off a node while the bootloader is being written. An interrupted write can leave it unbootable until you recover it over USB.
Create backup in the Provisioning group captures the node's drive as an image you can put back later. See Backups and golden images. Next: Working with a node.
See what a node is, run commands on it, open a terminal, track its files and remove it. Click a node on Nodes to open its panel. Everything you do to one device starts here.

Overview shows the node's state, addresses, versions and hardware. When a newer agent exists, Update appears next to Agent . Properties holds the node's name and its settings, each with its own page: boot behavior, credentials, secrets and attributes, utilities and hardware.

On Actions , Reboot to recovery network-boots the recovery system once, and Shutdown keeps the device off until someone powers it on. A new hostname applies without a reboot. Click Refresh DHCP lease to make DNS pick up the new name now. A manager may reboot, identify, rename and run playbooks. Shutting down, deleting, the terminal, file edits and agent updates need an admin. Identify blinks the board's activity LED for 5 minutes, or for the time set on the Account page. Click ID in the node list to stop it early. There is no script box. A script runs as a step of a playbook: 1. Click Run playbook . 2. Pick an active playbook that covers this node. 3. Click Run playbook . Each step's output is in the run's details under Operations . See Playbooks. What a command's status means Command history shows the last 20 commands. Status Meaning registered Accepted, waiting for delivery. sent / in_progress Delivered / running on the device. success / failed Finished. A failure adds What the node reported . superseded A newer command of the same kind replaced it before delivery. expired Waited 24 hours for an offline node and was dropped. skipped Not applied on purpose, for example because the agent is too old. Reboot, shutdown, scripts, file reads and installs fail at once on an offline node. Settings and agent updates wait for it to reconnect, and most also wait until it boots its installed OS.

Click Terminal for a root shell. It runs over the agent's connection, so the device needs no open SSH port, and it works in the recovery system too. Type exit or click ← Back to close it. The row appears only if the install sets TERMINAL_ENABLED . It is off by default and on in the community compose file (CONFIGURATION.md). Admins and Super Admins can use it, and a Super Admin can grant it to other roles under Role permissions (Team and security). If the account requires two-factor authentication, yours must be enrolled. The server closes the shell within a minute if you lose access. The audit trail records opening and closing, but not keystrokes.

1. Open Advanced → Files and click Add file . 2. Enter the file's absolute path. The platform reads it and stores version 1. 3. Click the file, change Content and click Save version . 4. Click Apply to device . Refresh from device stores a new version when the file changed on the device. The password-hash files, the adoption file and files ending in .pem , .key , .p12 or .pfx are refused. Don't track any other file that holds a secret either. A version holds at most 512 KiB, and anyone who can manage the node's files can read it. /boot/firmware/config.txt is tracked on every node as MANAGED . You can edit it but not untrack it. To stop tracking another file, click Untrack (keep the file on the device) . Delete on device removes the file and keeps a backup beside it.

Actions → Delete node deletes the node's command history, tracked files and secret attachments. A connected device erases its adoption file and keeps its users, keys, data and agent. To remove the agent too, run the uninstall script from INSTALL.md. An offline device is not told and keeps trying to connect with an identity the platform refuses. To swap hardware instead, Replace with another node moves the attributes, hostname and unit onto a spare node. Set the status filter on Nodes to Deleted to find deleted nodes. Restore gives the identity back, so the device is accepted again. History and files do not return. If the board has since joined as another node in your account, Restore is disabled and the panel names that node. Delete it first to take the old one back. Forget removes the record for good. Warning: A device set up for network boot keeps its node credential in the bootloader, and Restore makes it valid again. To revoke it, delete the node and then Forget it. Next: Hardware profiles, overclocking and the watchdog.

p: Hardware profiles, overclocking and the watchdog
t: Tell the server what hardware a node has, overclock it, and let a hung node reset itself. Declare a node's hardware, overclock it or arm its watchdog from the node's Properties and Advanced tabs. None of these reboots the node for you.

p: Hardware profiles, overclocking and the watchdog
h: Tell the server what board and add-ons a node has
t: The server detects the compute module. It cannot see the carrier board, or a clock or TPM chip that stays invisible until its overlay loads. A hardware profile declares them. 1. Open the node and go to Properties → Platform . 2. Choose a board. The list shows only boards that fit the detected module, and Inherit follows the unit or account. 3. Pick the Variant and any Modules . 4. Click Apply . The confirmation shows the block that will be written into config.txt. 5. Click Reboot . 6. Click Scan . After the scan, confirmed or works means the hardware answers. not found means a wrong variant, a module not seated, or no reboot since the apply. A wrong declaration does no harm. Modules that clash on pins, I2C address or bus are refused when you save. An apply to an offline node waits until the node connects on its installed OS. Scan is refused while the node runs the recovery system. To declare hardware for a whole unit, use the Hardware section of its policies and click Apply hardware profile to N nodes (Organizational units and policies).

p: Hardware profiles, overclocking and the watchdog
t: 1. Open Advanced → Overclock . 2. Select Stock , Balanced or Performance . 3. Click Apply (for example Apply balanced preset ). 4. Reboot the node. Nothing changes until the reboot. An offline node gets the change when it reconnects. Apply preset stays disabled until you select a preset. On a Pi 5 or CM5, Balanced is 2.6 GHz at stock voltage and Performance 2.8 GHz. On a Pi 4 or CM4 they are 1.8 and 2.0 GHz. Stock removes the overclock. No preset uses force_turbo , so the board still slows down when idle or hot. Check the cooling before you use Performance . Warning: An unstable overclock can stop the board from booting its OS. If the install has the boot-loop failsafe on ( PROVISIONING_BOOT_FAILSAFE_THRESHOLD , off by default), the node falls back to the recovery system, so apply Stock and reboot. Otherwise boot it from SD or USB media and delete the overclock block from config.txt.

p: Hardware profiles, overclocking and the watchdog
h: Let a hung node reset itself
t: The watchdog reboots the node when a check you choose fails. A new node has none armed. 1. Open Advanced → Watchdog . 2. Pick a preset. Watch the agent is the safest start. 3. Click Arm this configuration and confirm. Watch the OS reboots on a kernel hang and takes effect after the next reboot. Watch the network reboots when the address you type stops answering. Custom configuration… lets you set every check yourself. The device refuses a configuration that would reboot it straight away, such as an unreachable ping target, and the panel shows "Device refused to arm: …". Disarm the watchdog stops supervision. A unit's Watchdog policy arms nothing until you click Arm the inherited configuration on each node. If a node restarts three times, each within 20 minutes of the last boot, it disarms its own watchdog. The node list then shows WATCHDOG OFF . Find out why it kept restarting, then click Re-arm . Don't arm it: - during a long package upgrade, because arming installs the watchdog package with apt and fails while apt is busy. - with Watch the network pointed at something you don't control. An outage there reboots every node watching it. - with Watch the OS while a kernel or firmware update is pending, unless you reboot once and watch the node come back before you leave it.

p: Hardware profiles, overclocking and the watchdog
t: Properties → LEDs turns off the activity and power LEDs, and on a Compute Blade adds Stealth mode and Digital LED indication . The settings do not apply in the recovery system, and identify is on the node's Actions tab (Working with a node). Next: Organizational units and policies, to set these once for a whole unit.

Copy a node's drive to the server, put it back, or turn it into an image for other nodes. Copy a node's drive to your server and put it back later, or turn a configured node into a golden image you install on other nodes. Both are taken while the node runs the recovery system.

1. Open the node, go to Actions and click Reboot to recovery . Wait until it shows RECOVERY . 2. Under Provisioning , click Create backup . 3. Type an Image title . Leave Target Device on Boot disk (default) unless the system lives on another drive. 4. Leave Golden image unticked and click Create backup . 5. Open Command history and wait until Capture image reads SUCCESS . 6. Click Reboot . The node starts its own system again, because Reboot to recovery lasts for one boot. The capture checks the filesystem, shrinks it to its data, then reads and uploads the drive. The terminal is unavailable while it runs. A fresh Ubuntu on a 1 TB drive came to 1.8 GB and took about six minutes. The backup appears under Operations → Backups . Click it to see which node it was captured from, download it or delete it.

1. Reboot the node to recovery. 2. Under Provisioning , click Restore from backup . 3. In Image , pick the backup. Backups and golden images are listed after the OS images. 4. Pick the Target Device and click Restore from backup . 5. Read the confirmation and click Restore from backup again. 6. When Command history shows the install has finished, click Reboot . Warning: A restore erases the target drive. Everything written since the backup is lost. The node stays in recovery after the restore until you reboot it. Check that Properties → Boot behavior reads Local OS before you do. Restored onto the same node, a backup boots as that node. Restored onto a different node, the server strips the machine identity during the install so the copy doesn't clash with its source.

h: Make a golden image and install it on other nodes
t: A golden image is a backup without the machine identity: machine-id, SSH host keys, the adoption file, network state and hostname. Set up one node the way you want every node, then capture it. 1. Reboot the configured node to recovery. 2. Click Create backup , give it a title and tick Golden image . 3. Click Create backup and wait for SUCCESS . The source node keeps its own identity. 4. Reboot the source node. 5. On each target node, follow Installing an operating system and pick the golden image in Image . Golden images are listed under Operations → Gold images .

h: What a backup holds and where it lives
t: A backup covers the drive up to the end of the system partition, with free space trimmed, stored compressed. It restores onto a smaller or larger drive as long as the data fits. A drive with a partition after the system partition can't be captured. Backups and golden images live in your server's image storage, on local disk or in the bucket if the server uses object storage. They count toward the image limits set by whoever runs the server ( IMAGE_MAX_PER_ACCOUNT , IMAGE_MAX_BYTES_PER_ACCOUNT , IMAGE_MAX_BYTES_INSTANCE in CONFIGURATION.md). Nothing deletes them for you.
Admins can create and restore backups. Downloading or deleting an image needs the account's Super Admin. A backup carries the node's credentials, so treat a downloaded copy as a secret.

Group nodes into units and set policies once for all of them. Units group nodes, such as the devices in one room or one site. Anything you set on a unit reaches every node in it, including nodes you move in later. A node's own setting wins, then its unit's, then a parent unit's if the unit is nested, then the account default. SSH users, secrets and utilities attached at several levels add up on the node. Where two levels define the same user, secret or utility, the nearer level wins.

1. Open Organization in the top bar. 2. Click + New OU under the tree. 3. Type a Name . 4. Choose a Parent , or leave None for a top-level unit. Units nest two levels deep. 5. Click Create . Rename a unit with the pencil next to its name. Drag it in the rail onto another unit to change its parent. Delete unit refuses while the unit still holds nodes, child units, playbooks or utility assignments. Move those out first.

1. Open Nodes . 2. Click Select / Assign to unit above the table. 3. Tick the nodes. 4. Open Assign to unit and pick the unit. You can also drag selected rows onto a unit in the left rail, or use Move on the Unit row of a node's Overview . A moved node picks up the new unit's settings at once. To place new devices in a unit when they join, give their adoption token an Adoption OU (Secrets and variables).

h: Set a policy on a unit or for the whole account
t: 1. Open Organization . 2. Select a unit in the rail, or Account defaults for every node that has no answer of its own. 3. On the Policies tab, change the fields you need. 4. Click Save policies . A field left on Inherit shows the value that applies and where it comes from, for example Effective: Recovery (netboot) (from system default) . What you can set: - Target , the system a node boots (Install an OS) - Auto-flash EEPROM on approval - Password login (Access) - Default image , the OS image an install uses when it names none - Platform , the board, its variant, LEDs and modules (Hardware and watchdog) - Supervision , the watchdog (Hardware and watchdog) Password login goes to the devices as soon as you save. Saving hardware or watchdog settings only stores them, and nothing changes on a device until you apply them. The unit's Contents tab lists its nodes and everything that reaches them. N override(s) next to a node means it sets some fields itself, and Reset to inherited clears them. Next: Access: SSH keys and device users.

p: Access: SSH keys and device users
t: Add your SSH keys and create the Linux users your nodes should have. On Credentials you add SSH keys and create the Linux users the agent maintains on your nodes. Which nodes get a user is decided by the unit rules on Organizational units and policies.

p: Access: SSH keys and device users
t: 1. Open Credentials and the SSH Keys tab. 2. Click Add SSH key . 3. Under Paste public key , type an Alias . 4. Paste one public key line, such as ssh-ed25519 … . 5. Click Create Key . A value with several lines saves, but the device refuses it. A key grants nothing until you attach it to a user. Generate keypair creates a key the platform uses to adopt devices over the network. You don't log in with it.

p: Access: SSH keys and device users
h: Create a user on a unit
t: 1. Open the Users tab. 2. Select the unit in the left rail, or All nodes for the whole account. 3. Click Add user . 4. Type the Username . 5. Tick or clear Grant sudo . 6. Pick your key under SSH keys and click Attach . 7. Click Create user . A sudo user with no password gets sudo without a prompt on every node in its scope. Set a Password if you want one. The device only ever receives a salted hash of it. Click a user to change it. Changes in that panel save at once.

p: Access: SSH keys and device users
t: The account appears on online nodes right away and on offline nodes when they reconnect. A node in the recovery system gets it once it is back on its installed OS. Deleting a user locks the account on its nodes and keeps the home directory. The same happens when a user loses its last key and has no password. Accounts you created by hand on a node are never touched. To check one node, open it and go to Properties → Credentials . Scan lists the real accounts on its disk, marked managed or unmanaged . Warning: Before you set Password login to Refused (keys only) , log in to one of the unit's nodes with your key. If the key doesn't work, those nodes become unreachable over SSH. If you do lock yourself out, add a key or a password to a user in that scope. The change reaches the node over the agent's own connection.

p: Access: SSH keys and device users
h: Trust a CA for certificate logins
t: Add your certificate authority's public key on CA Certificates and drag it onto a unit or All nodes . A node then accepts a certificate signed by that CA when it names one of a user's Certificate principals . Next: Secrets and variables.

Store values once and use them on your nodes and in playbooks. On Secrets you store a value once, attach it where it is needed and use it as {{secrets.NAME}} . Only Admins and Super Admins see this page. Use a variable for URLs, time zones and settings: it stays readable and editable. Use a secret for passwords and keys: its value is hidden on this page once you save it. Admins and Super Admins can still see the value in the commands and playbook runs that used it. Which nodes an attached value reaches is decided by the unit rules on Organizational units and policies.

h: Add a variable or a secret
t: 1. Open Secrets and click Create secret . 2. Type a Name . It is the name you use in {{secrets.NAME}} . 3. Choose the Kind . Env writes the value to the device as an environment variable. Credential and Opaque are used only by playbooks. 4. Tick Non-sensitive variable for a variable, or leave it clear for a secret. 5. Fill in the ENV name, username or label, and the Value . 6. Click Create Secret . Convert to secret turns a variable into a secret and can't be undone.

h: Attach it to a unit, a node or a tag
t: A new entry goes nowhere until you attach it. Pick one way: - Drag its row onto a unit in the left rail. - On a node, open Properties → Secrets and search for it. - Give it a tag on the Tags tab, then attach the tag to a unit or node. Everything carrying the tag goes there, including entries you tag later. When two entries with the same name reach one node, the nearer level wins. Within one level, a direct attachment beats a tag. The node's Secrets view shows what it receives and from where. Env entries land in /etc/orchestrator/env , which only root can read. Load them in a systemd service with EnvironmentFile=/etc/orchestrator/env . Agents older than 0.8.5 write them to /etc/environment , where every login session can read them, so update those agents before you attach secrets.

h: Use a value in a playbook
t: Write {{secrets.NAME}} in any text parameter of a playbook step. The server fills it in when the step runs, from the entries that reach that node. Utility parameters accept variables only. A secret is refused there. Warning: A changed value reaches a device's env file only when the node's access is provisioned again, which happens at an OS install. Playbooks use the new value from their next run. Keep an old credential valid until every node has the new one.

The Tokens tab holds master tokens, which new devices present to join your account. One is created for you when you generate a one-command install or download the master image bundle, and Create token makes one by hand. A token is a secret. Anyone holding it, or an SD card built with it, can join devices to your account until it expires, so Deactivate tokens you no longer need. Next: Utilities: managed software.

Assign built-in software to a unit and keep it installed and configured. A utility is software from a built-in catalog that the platform installs and keeps configured on every node its assignment reaches. Which nodes those are is decided by the unit rules on Organizational units and policies.

h: Assign a utility to a unit
t: 1. Open Utilities and the Assignments tab. 2. Select the unit in the left rail. 3. Click Assign utility and pick one. 4. Set the parameters in the panel that opens. 5. Click Save . 6. Click Apply . Apply sends what is saved, so save first. Online nodes get it at once and offline nodes when they reconnect. A node you approve later gets its unit's utilities at once. Text parameters can use {{secrets.NAME}} for variables and {{node.attributes.KEY}} . A secret is refused, because a utility's settings can be read back from the device. A node needs its installed OS, a Debian-based system and agent 0.6.5 or newer to receive utilities.

Open the node, then Properties → Utilities . applied means the device confirmed this configuration. update pending means it changed since, declared means it was never applied, and failed shows the reason on hover. Apply now resends this node's whole set.

Click Delete on the assignment. The software stays installed and keeps running, and the platform stops managing it. To uninstall it, run a playbook. Clear Enabled and save to pause an assignment without losing its settings.

- Docker : the Docker engine, with log rotation. Members of the docker group are effectively root. - Kiosk display : one web page fullscreen on HDMI. Brings Docker along. - Metrics exporter : Prometheus node exporter on port 9100, without authentication. - Storage endurance : less SD-card wear, with zram swap and a journal cap. - Tailscale VPN : joins your tailnet. Use a short-lived auth key. - Security updates : automatic security updates. It never reboots, so reboot yourself after a kernel update. - ZeroTier network : joins a ZeroTier network.

h: Example: put a dashboard on a screen
t: 1. On Secrets , create a variable KIOSK_URL with the dashboard address and attach it to the unit. 2. On Utilities , select the unit and assign Kiosk display . 3. Set URL to {{secrets.KIOSK_URL}} , leave Kiosk image on the default and click Save . 4. Click Apply . 5. On a node with a screen, open Properties → Utilities and check that Kiosk display shows applied . A changed KIOSK_URL reaches the screens at the next Apply . To show another page on one screen, assign the kiosk to that node too. The node's assignment wins. Next: Status, attention and the audit trail.

p: Status, attention and the audit trail
t: See which nodes need you, fix them in bulk, and find what was sent and who did what. Open Status → Attention to see every node that needs you. The number next to Status in the top bar counts open conditions, so one node can count twice.

p: Status, attention and the audit trail
t: Click a chip to show only the nodes with that condition. To fix several at once: 1. Tick the nodes, or click Select all . 2. Click the action in the bar above the table, for example Update agent 2 . 3. Confirm. The results list each node as Sent , Queued , Skipped or Failed . The number on the action counts only the nodes it can reach. A node still carrying an earlier command shows Running , so wait for that command to finish first. Condition What to do Offline Check power and network. Queued commands wait for it. Not back yet , Waiting to leave recovery Usually wait. Never connected Check the device was flashed and has network (Adding a device). Waiting for approval Approve , or reject it in the node panel. Agent update available Update agent . Bootloader update available Update bootloader , then reboot. Bootloader flashed, reboot to apply , Hardware profile applied, reboot to bring it up Reboot when it suits you. Hardware profile not applied Apply profile . Utility not applied Apply utilities (Utilities). Device login setup failed Fix the cause, then Re-apply (Access and credentials). In recovery Finish the work there, or boot the OS (Installing an OS). Failing to boot , Sent to recovery after failed boots Find why the OS won't boot. Then Acknowledge the recovery mark. Watchdog disarmed by the device Find why it kept restarting, then re-arm (Hardware and watchdog). Unit no longer exists Move the node to an existing unit. Watcher cannot netboot Fix the boot order at the device. Device credential unreadable Fix the server's keys (configuration reference). Command stopped reporting Check the node's command history. Device limit reached Open subscription , or delete a node. Hide stops counting a node's conditions in this browser until one of them changes. If a check could not run, for example because the agent release list was unreachable, a line above the table names it.

p: Status, attention and the audit trail
h: Find a command that was sent
t: Status → Logs lists every command sent to any node, whether you, a playbook or the platform sent it. Filter it by status, time window and command name, and click a row to open that node's panel. Replaced , Expired and Skipped are not failures. Details that may hold secret values read [redacted — requires secret.read_value] .

p: Status, attention and the audit trail
t: Open the account menu, then Account → Audit . Only a Super Admin sees this tab. It lists every privileged action, such as secrets read, commands sent, terminals opened, playbooks started and members changed. Filter by action takes an exact name such as playbook.run_start . Actions the platform took on its own show the platform as the actor. Entries carry no source address. Nothing in the UI can delete an event.

p: Status, attention and the audit trail
t: Audit events are kept 365 days by default ( AUDIT_EVENT_RETENTION_DAYS , 0 keeps them forever), and the line above the list shows this account's value. To keep them longer, export them with GET /api/v1/audit-events before they age out. Command history is kept forever by default ( NODE_COMMAND_RETENTION_DAYS ) and 90 days in the community compose file. A command still waiting for delivery is never deleted. Finished playbook runs are kept 30 days. Next: Playbooks.
Build a list of steps once, then run it on the nodes you pick or on a schedule. You build playbooks on the Operations page and run them by hand or on a schedule.

The quickest start is an example. Open Operations , then the Playbooks tab. 1. Click From example . 2. Click a card: Install OS , Capture a golden image , Back up a node or Restore from a backup . 3. Review the steps in the editor. 4. Set Status to Active and click Save . An example is created as a draft. A draft is saved but never offered for a run and never fires on a schedule. To build one from scratch: 1. Click Create playbook . 2. Type a name into Playbook name . 3. Click a block in the Blocks palette. 4. Fill in its Parameters and click Add to canvas . It is added below the last step. 5. Repeat for each step. 6. Pick Active or Draft next to Status and click Create . Each block's Policy sets Retries , Timeout (s) and On error . Fail the run stops this node's run at the failed step. Continue goes on to the next one. Import takes a JSON file exported from another playbook and creates it as a draft. Pick OS images and SSH keys again after importing, because export strips them. A new playbook is available on all nodes. To limit it to a unit, drag its row onto that unit in the rail on the left. Drop it on All playbooks to undo that. Use secrets and node values Write {{secrets.NAME}} in a text field to use a secret or variable that reaches the node (see Secrets and variables). Node values work the same way, for example {{node.hostname}} or {{node.attributes.KEY}} . An unknown reference becomes an empty string.

Blocks marked destructive in red can lose data or interrupt service. - Reboot , Shutdown : power the node. - Install OS , Capture image : write or save a disk image. - Install agent , Update agent : manage the agent. - Install packages , Manage service : software and systemd units. - Download file , Write file , Update file , Read file , Wait for file : work with files. - Patch config file , Patch file (from recovery) : edit a managed block in a file. - Run script : run a shell script and capture its output. - Set hostname , Provision access , Set watchdog : system settings. - Update boot order , Set boot policy , Reboot to recovery , Allow EEPROM flashing from the OS : boot settings. - Erase drive : wipe a drive. - Status check : collect the node's state. - Wait for node , Wait , Condition , Join : control the flow. - Save secret , Set node attribute , HTTP request : pass data to other systems. The editor warns when a block needs a boot state the steps before it do not reach, such as Capture image without Reboot to recovery and Wait for node .

1. On the Playbooks tab, hover the row and click the run icon. From a node, use Run playbook in its panel. 2. Tick the nodes. Only nodes inside the playbook's scope are listed. 3. If the playbook reboots or contains a destructive block, tick I understand what this will do to the selected nodes . 4. Click Run on N nodes . Each node runs its own copy in parallel, so one failing node does not stop the others. A run uses the playbook as it was when the run started. On an offline node, scripts, reboots and file reads fail at once, while Set hostname , Patch config file and Update agent wait in the node's queue for up to 24 hours.

1. Open the Runs tab. 2. Click a run to open Run details . 3. Click Show output to see each step's result, with EXIT_CODE , STDERR and STDOUT for scripts. Each node has a bar with one segment per step. Green succeeded, orange is running, red failed. Here a Collect diagnostics run on rocket-bench-01 failed with script exited with code 3 . Show output shows that the step Check free disk space failed, and its STDERR says why: Not enough free disk space: 443 GB free on /, at least 1000 GB required . After fixing the playbook, click Retry 1 failed node to run the current version on the failed nodes only. Cancel run in Run details stops a run immediately, without asking. Cancelling does not stop a command already running on the device, so a script started before you cancelled runs to its end.

1. Open the playbook and select the Start block. 2. Set Trigger to On a schedule . 3. Pick a preset under Cron expression , or Custom for a five-field cron expression. 4. Click Save . Schedules are in UTC. The panel shows the next runs in UTC and in your local time. A scheduled run targets every node in the playbook's scope, offline ones included. Next: Team, sign-in security and the device limit.
Sign in from a script, then list nodes, send commands, start playbooks and read the results. Everything the web UI does goes through an HTTP API, so a script can do the same.

Through the bundled proxy the base URL is https://<your server /api , or http://<your server /api on a local-network install. Versioned routes have /api twice, as in /api/api/v1/nodes , because the proxy strips the first one before the request reaches the server. Every route and field is in backend/docs/swagger.json in the release tree. A production server does not serve a browsable API page.

h: Sign in and get a token
t: API=https://orchestrator.example.com/api read -rs PASSWORD LOGIN=$(printf '{"email":"automation@example.com","password":"%s"}' "$PASSWORD" curl -fsS -X POST "$API/auth/login" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @-) TOKEN=$(jq -r .data.access_token <<<"$LOGIN") REFRESH=$(jq -r .data.refresh_token <<<"$LOGIN") Piping the body keeps the password out of the process list. Send the token as Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN . It lasts 15 minutes. Exchange the refresh token for a new pair before then: NEXT=$(printf '{"refresh_token":"%s"}' "$REFRESH" curl -fsS -X POST "$API/auth/refresh" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @-) A 202 answer means sign-in is not finished. With two_factor_required , send the two_factor_token and an authenticator code to POST /api/auth/2fa . With account selection required , the user belongs to several accounts, so send the pre_token and one account_id to POST /api/auth/select-account . There are no long-lived API keys in this release. A script signs in as a member. Create a dedicated member for it and give it the smallest role that does the job (Team and security). Reboots, identify and plain playbooks need Manager . Scripts, privileged playbooks and reading script output need Admin . The audit trail needs Super Admin . The tokens under Secrets → Tokens enrol new devices. They do not sign in to the API.
curl -fsS "$API/api/v1/nodes?search=bench&page=1&per_page=50" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" jq '.data.nodes[] {id, name, status, ipv4}' Add ou_id=<unit-id for the nodes directly in a unit.

Blink the node's LED: curl -fsS -X POST "$API/api/v1/nodes/<node-id /identify" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"duration_sec":60}' {"success":true,"data":{"command_id":"<command-id ","duration_sec":60},...} Run a script, then poll its command: CMD=$(curl -fsS -X POST "$API/api/v1/nodes/<node-id /command" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"command":"run_script","params":{"script":"df -h /","timeout_seconds":30}}' jq -r .data.command_id) curl -fsS "$API/api/v1/node-commands/$CMD" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" jq '.data {status, result}' {"status":"success","result":{"exit_code":"0","stdout":"Filesystem ...","stderr":""}} status moves through registered , sent and in_progress . It ends as success , failed , superseded , expired or skipped . A non-zero exit code fails the command. The other commands and their parameters are in the device commands reference.

h: Start a playbook and read the run
t: Find the playbook's id, then start it on the nodes you name: curl -fsS "$API/api/v1/workflow-templates?name=Nightly" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" jq '.data[] {id, name}' RUN=$(curl -fsS -X POST "$API/api/v1/workflow-executions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"template_id":"<playbook-id ","node_ids":["<node-id "]}' jq -r .data.id) curl -fsS "$API/api/v1/workflow-executions/$RUN" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" jq '.data {status, nodes: [.nodes[] {node_id, status, error_message}]}' To run it on a unit, list the unit's nodes with ou_id and pass their ids. A run ends as completed , failed or partially_failed . A draft playbook answers 409.

curl -fsS "$API/api/v1/audit-events?action=node.delete&per_page=50" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" jq '.data.events[] {created_at, action, actor_user_id, target_id}' The audit trail filters by action and actor but not by time. For device commands since a moment, set SINCE to an RFC3339 time: curl -fsS "$API/api/v1/fleet/activity?since=$SINCE&status=failed" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" jq '.data.activity[] {created_at, node_name, slug, status}'

Routes that change who can sign in or what a member may do need an X-Reauth-Ticket header. These include inviting members, changing roles and the security settings. Get a ticket by sending the password again: TICKET=$(printf '{"password":"%s"}' "$PASSWORD" curl -fsS -X POST "$API/api/v1/users/me/reauth/password" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @- jq -r .data.ticket) The ticket lasts five minutes and works for several requests from the same session. Without it those routes answer 403 with "code": "reauth_required" .

- Too many failed sign-ins from one address answer 429 with login_throttled and a Retry-After header. - The /auth/ routes, refresh included, allow about 30 requests a minute per client address, with bursts of 10. Past that they answer 429 without a code. - A user holds at most 10 sessions, and each sign-in past that ends the oldest one. Reuse and refresh the token instead of signing in on every call. - The API allows 20 requests per second per account, with bursts of 100. - Most lists page with page and per_page (default 50, at most 200). - Errors carry success: false , a message and sometimes a code to act on. The node command route answers a refusal as {"error": <code , "message": …} instead.

p: Team, sign-in security and the device limit
t: Invite people, give them roles, protect your sign-in and see how many devices your server admits. Click your initials at the top right: Team Management holds the members, Account your own sign-in.

p: Team, sign-in security and the device limit
t: 1. Open Team Management . 2. Under Invite a member , type the address into Email and pick a role. 3. Click Create invite , then confirm it's you. 4. Without a mail server, copy the one-time link the page shows and hand it over through a channel you trust. With one, the person gets it by email. The link expires after seven days, and the pending invitation shows the date. Resend makes a new link and Revoke withdraws the invitation. To change a role later, pick another one in the member's selector. Disable suspends a member until you click Enable , and Remove takes them out of the account. Each change asks you to confirm, then takes effect at once.

p: Team, sign-in security and the device limit
t: Role May do Viewer See nodes, playbooks and utilities. No secrets, no commands. Manager Reboot nodes, set hostnames, run playbooks without privileged steps. Admin Install an OS, open the web terminal, manage secrets and run any playbook. Each role includes the one above it. A Super Admin can do everything, including managing members and the subscription. You can also grant a role on a single unit from the Organization page.

p: Team, sign-in security and the device limit
t: 1. Open Account . 2. Under Two-step verification , click Turn on , then confirm it's you. 3. Scan the QR code with your authenticator app. 4. Type the six-digit code into Code from your app and click Confirm . 5. Store the ten recovery codes away from your phone, then click I have saved them . Warning: The recovery codes are shown only once. The QR code, its key and each recovery code are enough to pass your second step, so keep them out of tickets and screenshots. To make two-step sign-in mandatory for everyone, tick Require two-step verification in Team Management .

p: Team, sign-in security and the device limit
t: Sessions on Account lists every browser and script signed in as you. A browser shows as its browser and system, a script as Unknown device . Your current browser is marked this device . Hover over a row to see the full browser identification. Click Sign out on a row to end that session, or Sign out of my other sessions to end all but this one, then confirm. You can hold 10 sessions, and a new sign-in beyond that signs out the one used least recently. Give scripts their own user so they do not push your browser out.

p: Team, sign-in security and the device limit
t: Your own server admits 25 devices free, and a hosted account 10. The count is on Account → Subscription . To raise it on your own server, get an entitlement file at orchestrator.sh/subscription and apply it there. On the hosted service, write to sales@orchestrator.sh.

p: Team, sign-in security and the device limit
t: The operator resets a forgotten password or a lost authenticator from the server's command line (Recover a lost password or authenticator). Sign-in through an identity provider such as Google is off until the operator sets it up (Email and single sign-on). Next: Backup, restore and upgrading the server.

p: Backup, restore and upgrading the server
t: What to back up, where the restore and upgrade procedures are, and how to update agents. The commands for a self-hosted server are in the reference: BACKUP-RESTORE.md and INSTALL.md → Upgrading.

p: Backup, restore and upgrading the server
t: Paths are as in the community compose file. - The credential files in secrets/ . - The bootloader signing key, data/eeprom-keys/privkey.pem . - The database, as a nightly encrypted dump (A scripted nightly dump), copied off the host. - The key that encrypts your dumps, kept anywhere but the server. - The .env file beside the compose file. - OS images and agent releases in data/backend/storage/ or your bucket. - With the proxy-tls proxy, its certificate store data/proxy/acme.json . A local-network install has no certificate, and data/proxy/ stays empty. Warning: Without secrets/secrets_encryption_key the dump restores but nothing encrypted in it can be read. Without data/eeprom-keys/privkey.pem no server can sign a boot image your network-booting devices accept, so put both in an escrow you control before you adopt the first device.

p: Backup, restore and upgrading the server
t: The reference has two procedures, into the same install and onto an empty host, and the order of steps matters in both. Prepare an empty host by hand with the same release and DOMAIN , because the installer would create new keys and a new owner. Devices reconnect on their own when the restored server keeps the same name and keys.

p: Backup, restore and upgrading the server
t: The full procedure is INSTALL.md → Upgrading. 1. Read CHANGELOG.md for every release between yours and the new one. 2. Run the dump by hand and check your copies of secrets/ and .env . 3. Get the new release's files, run chmod -R a+rX proxy in the install directory, and create any new credential file its compose file names. 4. Set PLATFORM_VERSION in .env to the new release. 5. Run docker compose -f docker-compose.community.yml pull , then up -d , and check that every container is up. There is no downgrade across a schema change, so rolling back means restoring the dump from step 2.

p: Backup, restore and upgrading the server
t: The server hands devices the agent release you marked latest when you imported it ( --set-latest ). To update one node, open it and click Update in the Agent row on Overview , which works only while the node is online. To update many, open Status → Attention , filter by Agent update available , select the rows and click Update agent . A node offline at the time gets the update when it reconnects, and a node still finishing another command is held back until it is done.

- A card-booted device shows a login prompt and never appears. The card has a GUID partition table. In macOS Disk Utility, choose View → Show All Devices , select the card itself, erase it as MS-DOS (FAT) with scheme Master Boot Record , and unzip the bundle again. - A device another server managed ignores the card and boots its old system. Its bootloader tries network, NVMe, USB, then SD. Remove the drive while the card does its work, or flash the board from the browser. - The one command seems to hang on a new system. The system's first package upgrade holds the package manager, for up to about half an hour on a fresh Ubuntu. The script waits and names the process holding the lock once a minute. Leave it running. - The node appears as PENDING. A device from One command or Master image waits for approval. Open it, check the HW serial and click Approve . By default Admins and Super Admins can approve. - The backend log says adoption handshake rejected … node not found . The device presents an identity from another server or from a node you deleted. Flash it from the browser. If you adopted it again here, click Update bootloader on the new node.

h: A node is stuck in recovery or will not boot its system
t: - A device that already ran its own OS comes back in recovery. Its bootloader boots from this server, and its Boot behavior is Inherit , which means Recovery unless you changed the account default. Set it to Local OS in Properties and reboot. - A node boots into nothing, or into a system this server did not install. It is set to Local OS , and its drive holds no system with this server's agent. Set Boot behavior to Recovery and power-cycle it. Then install an OS and set Local OS . - Reboot to recovery is refused. The node is offline, or its bootloader does not try network boot first. Bring the node online, or click Update bootloader in Advanced → Bootloader / EEPROM . - A node goes offline on and off for up to half an hour after an OS install. The fresh system runs its first package upgrade, which restarts services. Wait. It settles when the upgrade ends.

h: A command or install does not finish
t: - Install OS shows an image but you can't pick it. The image has no uploaded file, no checksum yet, or is still being processed. The label says which. Wait, or upload the file in Operations → Install images . - Install OS fails with "device … is mounted". The node is using that drive. Check the Target Device and pick the drive you mean to erase. - Install OS fails during the download. The node tries an interrupted download up to three times by itself. If it still fails, run Install OS again. - After a failed install the node keeps booting recovery. It stays there until an install succeeds, so it never boots a half-written disk. Run Install OS and Install Agent again. - A command stays Queued. The node is offline. Changes of state wait up to a day: access, hostname, watchdog, LEDs, hardware profile, utilities, overclock and agent updates. A queued command that waits longer ends as Expired . A reboot, a script, an identify or an OS install fails at once instead. - Status shows "Command stopped reporting". A command the node accepted has said nothing for 30 minutes, usually because its report was lost. It settles when the node reconnects, for example after a power-cycle. - Restore of a deleted node is refused. Its board was adopted again as another node in this account, named in the deleted node's row. Delete that node first. - The uninstall script ends with NOT DONE . Another package operation held the package manager, so the agent package is still installed. Run the script again once that operation has finished.

- You forgot your password or lost your authenticator app. Use a recovery code if you saved them. Otherwise the operator resets it from the server's command line in one command (Recover a lost password or authenticator).

h: The server will not start after an upgrade
t: - The page loads but every request fails with 502. The backend refuses a database that a newer release has already migrated. Run docker compose -f docker-compose.community.yml logs backend grep -i schema in the install directory to see why. Go forward to the newer release again, or restore the backup you took before the upgrade. There is no downgrade. - After an upgrade, nothing answers on ports 443, 80 and 50051. The proxy cannot read its route files under proxy/ . Run chmod -R a+rX proxy in the install directory, with sudo if the files aren't yours, then docker restart orchestrator-proxy . - The browser shows a self-signed certificate. The proxy could not get its Let's Encrypt certificate. DOMAIN must resolve to this server from the internet, and port 80 must be open to it. docker logs orchestrator-proxy 2 &1 grep -i acme names the reason. Fix it, then run docker restart orchestrator-proxy . Let's Encrypt pauses a name for an hour after five failures.

1. Open the node and read Actions → Command history . A failed command says why. 2. Open Status → Attention (Status, attention and the audit trail). 3. On the server, run docker compose -f docker-compose.community.yml logs backend in the install directory. 4. Ask in the repository's issues. Report a security problem the private way SECURITY.md describes, never in an issue.
